4	
5	### Shealy & Stout (1993)
6	- **Title**: A Model-Based Standardization Approach that Separates True Bias/DIF from Group Ability Differences and Detects Test Bias/DTF as Well as Item Bias/DIF
7	- **Year**: 1993
8	- **Venue**: Psychometrika, 58(2), 159–194
9	- **Key method/finding**: Developed the SIBTEST procedure — a nonparametric, IRT model-based method that detects and estimates DIF without requiring item response function (IRF) estimation. Employs a regression correction technique to control inflated Type I error while separating true bias from group ability differences.

The multidimensional DIF framework directly informs our approach to separating genuine ability differences from item-specific anomalies.

12	### Clauser & Mazor (1998)
13	- **Title**: Using Statistical Procedures to Identify Differentially Functioning Test Items
14	- **Year**: 1998
15	- **Venue**: Educational Measurement: Issues and Practice, 17(1), 31–44
16	- **Key method/finding**: Comprehensive review of DIF detection methods including Mantel-Haenszel, logistic regression, and SIBTEST. Documents the landscape of statistical techniques for detecting items that function differently across groups while controlling for overall ability.
17	- **Relevance to our paper**: Provides the methodological taxonomy we draw from when selecting DIF detection procedures for the LLM benchmark setting. Establishes that multiple complementary DIF methods exist with different sensitivity profiles — motivating our multi-method approach.

19	### Zumbo (1999)
20	- **Title**: A Handbook on the Theory and Methods of Differential Item Functioning (DIF): Logistic Regression Modeling as a Unitary Framework for Binary and Likert-Type (Ordinal) Item Scores
21	- **Year**: 1999
22	- **Venue**: Technical report, Directorate of Human Resources Research and Evaluation, Department of National Defense, Ottawa, Canada
23	- **Key method/finding**: Presents logistic regression as a unifying framework for DIF analysis applicable to both binary and ordinal item scores. Provides theoretical grounding for understanding DIF as a violation of measurement invariance.
24	- **Relevance to our paper**: Our logistic-regression-based DIF detection for binary (correct/incorrect) LLM responses directly follows this framework. 26	### Holland & Wainer (1993)
27	- **Title**: Differential Item Functioning (edited volume)
28	- **Year**: 1993
29	- **Venue**: Lawrence Erlbaum Associates, Hillsdale, NJ
30	- **Key method/finding**: Definitive reference volume on DIF. 35	## 2. IRT in NLP/LLM Evaluation
36	
37	### Lalor, Wu & Yu (2016)
38	- **Title**: Building an Evaluation Scale using Item Response Theory
39	- **Year**: 2016
40	- **Venue**: EMNLP 2016, pp. 648–657
41	- **Key method/finding**: First to propose IRT as an alternative means for gold-standard test-set generation and NLP system evaluation. Applied to Recognizing Textual Entailment.
42	- **Relevance to our paper**: Pioneering work establishing that IRT is applicable to NLP evaluation. Our work extends this foundation from simple item characterization to cross-cohort equating and DIF detection.

44	### Lalor, Wu & Yu (2019)
45	- **Title**: Learning Latent Parameters without Human Response Patterns: Item Response Theory with Artificial Crowds
46	- **Year**: 2019
47	- **Venue**: EMNLP-IJCNLP 2019, Hong Kong
48	- **Key method/finding**: Addresses the bottleneck of needing human response patterns to calibrate IRT models by proposing to learn IRT parameters from "artificial crowds" of DNN models. 51	### Vania et al. (2021)
52	- **Title**: Comparing Test Sets with Item Response Theory
53	- **Year**: 2021
54	- **Venue**: ACL 2021
55	- **Key method/finding**: Evaluated 29 datasets using predictions from 18 pretrained Transformer models via IRT. 58	### Rodriguez et al. (2021)
59	- **Title**: Evaluation Examples Are Not Equally Informative: How Should That Change NLP Leaderboards?
60	- **Year**: 2021
61	- **Venue**: ACL-IJCNLP 2021
62	- **Key method/finding**: Creates a Bayesian IRT leaderboard model where latent subject skill and latent item difficulty predict correct responses. Demonstrates that IRT can guide annotation priorities, identify annotation errors, detect overfitting, and identify the most informative evaluation examples. Their Bayesian IRT approach to leaderboards establishes that item-level modeling reveals evaluation quality issues invisible to aggregate scores. We build on this by using IRT-derived item parameters to detect contamination-induced parameter drift.

66	- **Title**: tinyBenchmarks: Evaluating LLMs with Fewer Examples
67	- **Year**: 2024
68	- **Venue**: ICML 2024

78	- **Year**: 2024
79	- **Venue**: ICLR 2024

86	- **Venue**: ICLR 2025

90	### Balloccu et al. (2024)
91	- **Title**: Leak, Cheat, Repeat: Data Contamination and Evaluation Malpractices in Closed-Source LLMs
92	- **Year**: 2024
93	- **Venue**: EACL 2024
94	- **Key method/finding**: Systematic review of 255 papers using ChatGPT/GPT-4, documenting that over 4.7M samples from 263 datasets were exposed through the web interface. Catalogs evaluation malpractices including unfair baselines, reproducibility issues, and lack of contamination awareness.

98	- **Title**: Data Contamination Quiz: A Tool to Detect and Estimate Contamination in Large Language Models
99	- **Year**: 2024
100	- **Venue**: TACL 2024
101	- **Key method/finding**: Frames contamination detection as a multiple-choice quiz: given an original instance and three word-level perturbations, a contaminated model should identify the original. 105	- **Title**: Proving Test Set Contamination in Black Box Language Models
106	- **Year**: 2024
107	- **Venue**: ICLR 2024

123	- **Title**: DyVal: Dynamic Evaluation of Large Language Models for Reasoning Tasks
124	- **Year**: 2024
125	- **Venue**: ICLR 2024
126	- **Key method/finding**: Generates evaluation tasks at test time using graph-based complexity control to mitigate memorization. Applies graph complexity metrics to parameterize reasoning problem difficulty. Dynamically constructs evaluation instances rather than relying on static test sets.

130	- **Title**: Dynamic Evaluation of Large Language Models by Meta Probing Agents
131	- **Year**: 2024
132	- **Venue**: arXiv:2402.14865

137	- **Title**: LiveBench: A Challenging, Contamination-Free LLM Benchmark
138	- **Year**: 2024
139	- **Venue**: arXiv:2406.19314
140	- **Key method/finding**: Releases new questions monthly based on recent datasets, arXiv papers, news, and IMDb synopses. 144	- **Title**: MMLU-Pro: A More Robust and Challenging Multi-Task Language Understanding Benchmark
145	- **Year**: 2024
146	- **Venue**: NeurIPS 2024

152	- **Year**: 2024

162	- **Title**: Growing Pains: Extensible and Efficient LLM Benchmarking Via Fixed Parameter Calibration
163	- **Year**: 2026 (April)
164	- **Venue**: arXiv:2604.12843
165	- **Authors**: Eliya Habba, Itay Itzhak, Asaf Yehudai, Yotam Perlitz, Elron Bandel, Michal Shmueli-Scheuer, Leshem Choshen, Gabriel Stanovsky
166	
167	#### Method Details
168	- **IRT Model**: Multidimensional 2PL IRT (MIRT-2PL). Each item has a discrimination vector **a_i** and intercept **d_i**.
169	- **Calibration**: Fixed Parameter Calibration (FPC) — previously calibrated item parameters are held fixed; only new item parameters are estimated when new benchmarks are added.
170	- **Anchor Selection**: Clustering-based method (following Polo et al.) that distributes anchors across the difficulty/discrimination space. Uses 100 anchor items per dataset. Outperforms top-K discrimination selection.
171	- **Scale**: 400+ models, evaluated on Open LLM Leaderboard (ARC, GSM8K, HellaSwag, MMLU, TruthfulQA, WinoGrande) and MMLU's 57 subjects.
172	- **Performance**: Predicts full-evaluation performance within 2–3 percentage points; Spearman ρ ≥ 0.9 for ranking preservation.
173	
174	#### Technical Comparison with Our Approach
175	
176	| Dimension | Growing Pains | Our DIF Approach |
177	|-----------|---------------|------------------|
178	| **Goal** | Efficient, extensible benchmarking via FPC | Detect contamination-induced measurement distortion |
179	| **IRT model** | MIRT-2PL | 2PL (with DIF extensions) |
180	| **Core technique** | Fixed parameter calibration with anchor items | DIF analysis across temporal model cohorts |
181	| **Contamination** | Acknowledged as limitation ("anchors may become contaminated or saturated over time, requiring recalibration") but **not addressed** | Central focus — DIF detects which items are affected |
182	| **Item drift** | Not detected; assumes item parameters are stable | Explicitly models item parameter drift as DIF signal |
183	| **DIF analysis** | Not mentioned | Core methodology |
184	| **Granularity** | Dataset/benchmark level efficiency | Item-level contamination diagnostics |
185	| **Binary response** | Yes (limitation acknowledged) | Yes |
186	
187	#### Complementarity
188	Growing Pains and our work are highly complementary:
189	1. **They assume stable item parameters; we test that assumption.** Their FPC framework relies on anchor item parameters not drifting. Our DIF analysis can identify when this assumption breaks down due to contamination.
190	2. **They optimize evaluation efficiency; we diagnose evaluation validity.** Growing Pains reduces the number of items needed; we identify which items should be trusted.
191	3. **Their acknowledged limitation is our research question.** They note "anchors may become contaminated or saturated over time, requiring recalibration" but do not address it. We provide the diagnostic tool for exactly this problem.
192	4. **Integration pathway**: DIF-flagged items could be excluded from Growing Pains' anchor sets, making their FPC calibration more robust to contamination.
193	
194	### Kipnis et al. (2025) — METABENCH
195	- **Title**: MetaBench: A Sparse Benchmark for LLM Evaluation
196	- **Year**: 2025
197	- **Venue**: ICLR 2025
198	- **Key method/finding**: Distills six Open LLM Leaderboard benchmarks (ARC, GSM8K, HellaSwag, MMLU, TruthfulQA, WinoGrande) into <3% of their combined size using data from 5000+ LLMs. Uses Generalized Additive Models (GAM) to model subset-to-full-set relationships. Reconstructs benchmark scores with <0.9% MAE and leaderboard scores with <0.5% MAE. Provides two disjoint versions for repeated evaluation. Integrated into EleutherAI's lm-evaluation-harness.
199	- **Relevance to our paper**: METABENCH is our primary data source — we use their 5000+ model response matrices for IRT calibration and DIF analysis. Their item selection optimizes for predictive accuracy of aggregate scores; our DIF analysis adds a validity dimension by identifying which items remain measurement-invariant across model cohorts. Items selected by MetaBench that we flag as contaminated would suggest the sparse benchmark itself may be vulnerable to contamination effects.

## Overview

ConStat is a statistical method that tests for performance-based contamination in LLMs. It was presented as a NeurIPS 2024 paper.

## How It Works

Given a reference benchmark and reference models, it computes the likelihood of the observed performance of the model under the null hypothesis that the model is not contaminated. ConStat detects performance-based contamination by comparing a model's performance on a benchmark to its performance on a reference benchmark, identifying contamination if the model performs much better on the benchmark.

## Types of Contamination Detected

Different reference benchmarks test different types of contamination: rephrased samples test syntax-specific contamination, samples from the same distribution test sample-specific contamination, and different benchmarks for the same task test benchmark-specific contamination.

## Key Findings

ConStat was applied to diverse model architectures and contamination scenarios, finding high levels of contamination in multiple popular models including Mistral, Llama, Yi, and the top-3 Open LLM Leaderboard models. ConStat's performance remains strong even in challenging scenarios, such as when models are trained on rephrased data, which are designed to evade syntax-specific detection.

# Literature Survey for Related Work (D011)

## 1. Impact-vs-DIF Classics

### Shealy & Stout (1993)
- **Title**: A Model-Based Standardization Approach that Separates True Bias/DIF from Group Ability Differences and Detects Test Bias/DTF as Well as Item Bias/DIF
- **Year**: 1993
- **Venue**: Psychometrika, 58(2), 159–194
- **Key method/finding**: Developed the SIBTEST procedure — a nonparametric, IRT model-based method that detects and estimates DIF without requiring item response function (IRF) estimation. Uses a multidimensional IRT model to explain how individual items combine to produce differential test functioning (DTF) at the test level. Employs a regression correction technique to control inflated Type I error while separating true bias from group ability differences.
- **Relevance to our paper**: SIBTEST is the foundational statistical test for detecting item-level bias across groups. Our DIF-based contamination detection adapts this logic: instead of demographic groups, we compare "pre-contamination" vs. "post-contamination" model cohorts. The multidimensional DIF framework directly informs our approach to separating genuine ability differences from item-specific anomalies.

### Clauser & Mazor (1998)
- **Title**: Using Statistical Procedures to Identify Differentially Functioning Test Items
- **Year**: 1998
- **Venue**: Educational Measurement: Issues and Practice, 17(1), 31–44
- **Key method/finding**: Comprehensive review of DIF detection methods including Mantel-Haenszel, logistic regression, and SIBTEST. Documents the landscape of statistical techniques for detecting items that function differently across groups while controlling for overall ability.
- **Relevance to our paper**: Provides the methodological taxonomy we draw from when selecting DIF detection procedures for the LLM benchmark setting. Establishes that multiple complementary DIF methods exist with different sensitivity profiles — motivating our multi-method approach.

### Zumbo (1999)
- **Title**: A Handbook on the Theory and Methods of Differential Item Functioning (DIF): Logistic Regression Modeling as a Unitary Framework for Binary and Likert-Type (Ordinal) Item Scores
- **Year**: 1999
- **Venue**: Technical report, Directorate of Human Resources Research and Evaluation, Department of National Defense, Ottawa, Canada
- **Key method/finding**: Presents logistic regression as a unifying framework for DIF analysis applicable to both binary and ordinal item scores. Provides theoretical grounding for understanding DIF as a violation of measurement invariance.
- **Relevance to our paper**: Our logistic-regression-based DIF detection for binary (correct/incorrect) LLM responses directly follows this framework. Zumbo's formalization of uniform vs. non-uniform DIF maps onto our distinction between items that are uniformly easier for contaminated models vs. items showing interaction effects with model ability.

### Holland & Wainer (1993)
- **Title**: Differential Item Functioning (edited volume)
- **Year**: 1993
- **Venue**: Lawrence Erlbaum Associates, Hillsdale, NJ
- **Key method/finding**: Definitive reference volume on DIF. Covers methods for detecting test items that function differently across examinee groups, including Mantel-Haenszel, IRT-based methods, and standardization approaches. Establishes the conceptual distinction between item impact (legitimate group differences) and item bias (construct-irrelevant difficulty).
- **Relevance to our paper**: The impact-vs-bias distinction is the conceptual backbone of our work. We argue that contamination-inflated performance is analogous to construct-irrelevant easiness — a form of DIF where the "group" variable is exposure to benchmark data rather than demographics.

---

## 2. IRT in NLP/LLM Evaluation

### Lalor, Wu & Yu (2016)
- **Title**: Building an Evaluation Scale using Item Response Theory
- **Year**: 2016
- **Venue**: EMNLP 2016, pp. 648–657
- **Key method/finding**: First to propose IRT as an alternative means for gold-standard test-set generation and NLP system evaluation. Demonstrates that IRT can describe characteristics of individual items (difficulty, discriminating power) and account for these in estimating NLP system ability. Applied to Recognizing Textual Entailment.
- **Relevance to our paper**: Pioneering work establishing that IRT is applicable to NLP evaluation. Our work extends this foundation from simple item characterization to cross-cohort equating and DIF detection.

### Lalor, Wu & Yu (2019)
- **Title**: Learning Latent Parameters without Human Response Patterns: Item Response Theory with Artificial Crowds
- **Year**: 2019
- **Venue**: EMNLP-IJCNLP 2019, Hong Kong
- **Key method/finding**: Addresses the bottleneck of needing human response patterns to calibrate IRT models by proposing to learn IRT parameters from "artificial crowds" of DNN models. Finds medium-to-large positive correlations between parameters learned from human vs. machine response patterns for NLI and sentiment analysis.
- **Relevance to our paper**: Validates that IRT parameters estimated from machine (model) responses are meaningful and correlate with human-derived parameters. This justifies our use of LLM response matrices for IRT calibration.

### Vania et al. (2021)
- **Title**: Comparing Test Sets with Item Response Theory
- **Year**: 2021
- **Venue**: ACL 2021
- **Key method/finding**: Evaluated 29 datasets using predictions from 18 pretrained Transformer models via IRT. Found that Quoref, HellaSwag, and MC-TACO best distinguish among SOTA models, while SNLI, MNLI, and CommitmentBank are saturated. Provides a principled way to compare the discriminative quality of benchmark datasets.
- **Relevance to our paper**: Demonstrates IRT-based benchmark comparison at the dataset level. Our work extends this to item-level analysis across temporal model cohorts, using DIF to detect which specific items have degraded discriminative quality due to contamination.

### Rodriguez et al. (2021)
- **Title**: Evaluation Examples Are Not Equally Informative: How Should That Change NLP Leaderboards?
- **Year**: 2021
- **Venue**: ACL-IJCNLP 2021
- **Key method/finding**: Creates a Bayesian IRT leaderboard model where latent subject skill and latent item difficulty predict correct responses. Demonstrates that IRT can guide annotation priorities, identify annotation errors, detect overfitting, and identify the most informative evaluation examples. Released open-source IRT leaderboard code.
- **Relevance to our paper**: Directly relevant methodological predecessor. Their Bayesian IRT approach to leaderboards establishes that item-level modeling reveals evaluation quality issues invisible to aggregate scores. We build on this by using IRT-derived item parameters to detect contamination-induced parameter drift.

### Polo et al. (2024)
- **Title**: tinyBenchmarks: Evaluating LLMs with Fewer Examples
- **Year**: 2024
- **Venue**: ICML 2024
- **Key method/finding**: Shows that evaluating on ~100 curated IRT-selected items per benchmark is sufficient to accurately reproduce full-benchmark performance. Released IRT-based evaluation tools and tiny versions of Open LLM Leaderboard, MMLU, HELM, and AlpacaEval 2.0. Uses clustering-based item selection to ensure coverage of the difficulty/discrimination space.
- **Relevance to our paper**: tinyBenchmarks demonstrates the practical value of IRT for efficient evaluation. Their item selection methodology (clustering IRT representations) is adopted by Growing Pains for anchor selection. Our DIF analysis provides a complementary diagnostic: not just which items are informative, but which items have become unreliable due to contamination.

---

## 3. Contamination Detection

### Shi et al. (2024)
- **Title**: Detecting Pretraining Data from Large Language Models
- **Year**: 2024
- **Venue**: ICLR 2024
- **Key method/finding**: Proposes MIN-K% PROB — a membership inference method that identifies pretraining data by checking whether the k% of tokens with minimum probability under the LLM are unlikely enough. Introduces the WIKIMIA benchmark for evaluation. Achieves 7.4% improvement over prior methods. Applied to copyrighted book detection, contaminated example detection, and privacy auditing.
- **Relevance to our paper**: Min-K% operates at the instance level (is this text in the training data?) while our DIF approach operates at the item level across model populations (does this item behave differently for likely-contaminated models?). The approaches are complementary: Min-K% requires model access per instance; DIF requires only response matrices.

### Zhang et al. (2024) — Min-K%++
- **Title**: Min-K%++: Improved Baseline for Detecting Pre-Training Data from Large Language Models
- **Year**: 2024
- **Venue**: ICLR 2025
- **Key method/finding**: Extends Min-K% by measuring how sharply peaked the likelihood is around the input (analogous to curvature), using second-order statistics motivated by the connection between maximum likelihood training and the Hessian trace via score matching. More robust than zeroth-order signals.
- **Relevance to our paper**: Further develops the instance-level contamination detection paradigm. Our work offers an orthogonal, population-level signal that does not require per-instance likelihood computation.

### Balloccu et al. (2024)
- **Title**: Leak, Cheat, Repeat: Data Contamination and Evaluation Malpractices in Closed-Source LLMs
- **Year**: 2024
- **Venue**: EACL 2024
- **Key method/finding**: Systematic review of 255 papers using ChatGPT/GPT-4, documenting that over 4.7M samples from 263 datasets were exposed through the web interface. Catalogs evaluation malpractices including unfair baselines, reproducibility issues, and lack of contamination awareness.
- **Relevance to our paper**: Establishes the scale and severity of the contamination problem. Their documentation of widespread data leakage motivates our work: if contamination is pervasive and hard to prevent, we need methods to detect and account for it post-hoc — exactly what DIF provides.

### Golchin & Surdeanu (2024)
- **Title**: Data Contamination Quiz: A Tool to Detect and Estimate Contamination in Large Language Models
- **Year**: 2024
- **Venue**: TACL 2024
- **Key method/finding**: Frames contamination detection as a multiple-choice quiz: given an original instance and three word-level perturbations, a contaminated model should identify the original. Achieves 92–100% accuracy across seven datasets. Detects specific contamination in AG News, WNLI, and XSum for GPT-4.
- **Relevance to our paper**: DCQ is a clever per-model, per-instance detection method but requires generating perturbations and querying the model. Our DIF approach is purely observational — it works from existing response matrices without additional model queries or perturbation generation.

### Oren et al. (2024)
- **Title**: Proving Test Set Contamination in Black Box Language Models
- **Year**: 2024
- **Venue**: ICLR 2024
- **Key method/finding**: Statistical test comparing likelihood of a benchmark's canonical ordering vs. shuffled versions. Contaminated models find canonical orderings more likely due to memorized example order. Provides exact false positive guarantees without requiring access to pretraining data or model weights. Effective on models as small as 1.4B parameters with only 1000 examples.
- **Relevance to our paper**: Elegant black-box method with formal statistical guarantees. However, it detects dataset-level contamination (is the whole benchmark memorized?) rather than item-level contamination effects (which specific items are affected?). Our DIF approach provides item-level granularity.

### Deng et al. (2024)
- **Title**: Investigating Data Contamination in Modern Benchmarks for Large Language Models
- **Year**: 2024
- **Venue**: NAACL 2024, pp. 8706–8719
- **Key method/finding**: Proposes two methods: a retrieval-based system to find overlaps between benchmarks and pretraining corpora (for open-source LLMs), and Testset Slot Guessing (TS-Guessing) for proprietary LLMs. Finds ChatGPT and GPT-4 achieve 52% and 57% exact match rates in guessing missing MMLU options.
- **Relevance to our paper**: Demonstrates contamination in the exact benchmark (MMLU) we analyze. Their TS-Guessing evidence of MMLU contamination in GPT-4 provides ground-truth validation context for our DIF-based detection.

---

## 4. Dynamic/Adaptive Benchmarks

### Zhu et al. (2024a) — DyVal
- **Title**: DyVal: Dynamic Evaluation of Large Language Models for Reasoning Tasks
- **Year**: 2024
- **Venue**: ICLR 2024
- **Key method/finding**: Generates evaluation tasks at test time using graph-based complexity control to mitigate memorization. Applies graph complexity metrics to parameterize reasoning problem difficulty. Dynamically constructs evaluation instances rather than relying on static test sets.
- **Relevance to our paper**: Represents the "regenerate the benchmark" approach to contamination. Our work takes the complementary "detect and account for contamination in existing benchmarks" approach, which preserves historical comparability.

### Zhu et al. (2024b) — DyVal 2
- **Title**: Dynamic Evaluation of Large Language Models by Meta Probing Agents
- **Year**: 2024
- **Venue**: arXiv:2402.14865
- **Key method/finding**: Extends DyVal with Meta Probing Agents (MPA) inspired by psychometrics. Agents automatically transform original evaluation problems targeting three cognitive abilities: language understanding, problem solving, and domain knowledge. More generalizable than task-specific dynamic generation.
- **Relevance to our paper**: MPA's psychometric inspiration is conceptually aligned with our IRT-based approach, but they use psychometrics to generate new items while we use it to analyze existing items for contamination signals.

### White et al. (2024) — LiveBench
- **Title**: LiveBench: A Challenging, Contamination-Free LLM Benchmark
- **Year**: 2024
- **Venue**: arXiv:2406.19314
- **Key method/finding**: Releases new questions monthly based on recent datasets, arXiv papers, news, and IMDb synopses. All questions have verifiable, objective ground-truth answers enabling automatic scoring without LLM judges. Spans 18 tasks across 6 categories (Math, Reasoning, Data Analysis, Language, Coding, Instruction Following).
- **Relevance to our paper**: LiveBench's monthly refresh strategy prevents contamination prospectively. Our DIF method detects contamination retrospectively in static benchmarks. The approaches address different temporal windows: LiveBench prevents future contamination; we diagnose past contamination in widely-used benchmarks whose historical results we want to preserve.

### Wang et al. (2024) — MMLU-Pro
- **Title**: MMLU-Pro: A More Robust and Challenging Multi-Task Language Understanding Benchmark
- **Year**: 2024
- **Venue**: NeurIPS 2024
- **Key method/finding**: Enhances MMLU with harder, reasoning-focused questions and increases answer choices from 4 to 10, reducing random guessing success. Over 12K questions across 14 domains. GPT-4o achieves only 72.6%, and the gap between GPT-4o and GPT-4-Turbo widens from 1% (MMLU) to 9% (MMLU-Pro), showing better discriminative power.
- **Relevance to our paper**: MMLU-Pro addresses contamination by making a harder benchmark, but doesn't diagnose which original MMLU items are compromised. Our DIF analysis can quantify exactly which MMLU items have degraded, providing evidence for why harder replacements are needed and which content areas are most affected.

### Gema et al. (2024) — MMLU-Redux
- **Title**: Are We Done with MMLU?
- **Year**: 2024
- **Venue**: arXiv:2406.04127
- **Key method/finding**: Manual re-annotation of 5,700 MMLU questions reveals a 6.5% error rate. Error types include parsing mistakes, multiple correct answers, and missing context. Virology subset has 57% errors. Re-evaluation with corrected labels shows significant metric discrepancies and ranking shifts.
- **Relevance to our paper**: MMLU-Redux addresses data quality while our work addresses contamination — both are sources of measurement error. Items flagged by DIF analysis that are not contaminated may instead have quality issues, making these analyses complementary.

---

## 5. Key Technical Comparisons

### Habba, Itzhak, Yehudai, Perlitz, Bandel, Shmueli-Scheuer, Choshen & Stanovsky (2026) — Growing Pains
- **Title**: Growing Pains: Extensible and Efficient LLM Benchmarking Via Fixed Parameter Calibration
- **Year**: 2026 (April)
- **Venue**: arXiv:2604.12843
- **Authors**: Eliya Habba, Itay Itzhak, Asaf Yehudai, Yotam Perlitz, Elron Bandel, Michal Shmueli-Scheuer, Leshem Choshen, Gabriel Stanovsky

#### Method Details
- **IRT Model**: Multidimensional 2PL IRT (MIRT-2PL). Each item has a discrimination vector **a_i** and intercept **d_i**.
- **Calibration**: Fixed Parameter Calibration (FPC) — previously calibrated item parameters are held fixed; only new item parameters are estimated when new benchmarks are added.
- **Anchor Selection**: Clustering-based method (following Polo et al.) that distributes anchors across the difficulty/discrimination space. Uses 100 anchor items per dataset. Outperforms top-K discrimination selection.
- **Scale**: 400+ models, evaluated on Open LLM Leaderboard (ARC, GSM8K, HellaSwag, MMLU, TruthfulQA, WinoGrande) and MMLU's 57 subjects.
- **Performance**: Predicts full-evaluation performance within 2–3 percentage points; Spearman ρ ≥ 0.9 for ranking preservation.

#### Technical Comparison with Our Approach

| Dimension | Growing Pains | Our DIF Approach |
|-----------|---------------|------------------|
| **Goal** | Efficient, extensible benchmarking via FPC | Detect contamination-induced measurement distortion |
| **IRT model** | MIRT-2PL | 2PL (with DIF extensions) |
| **Core technique** | Fixed parameter calibration with anchor items | DIF analysis across temporal model cohorts |
| **Contamination** | Acknowledged as limitation ("anchors may become contaminated or saturated over time, requiring recalibration") but **not addressed** | Central focus — DIF detects which items are affected |
| **Item drift** | Not detected; assumes item parameters are stable | Explicitly models item parameter drift as DIF signal |
| **DIF analysis** | Not mentioned | Core methodology |
| **Granularity** | Dataset/benchmark level efficiency | Item-level contamination diagnostics |
| **Binary response** | Yes (limitation acknowledged) | Yes |

#### Complementarity
Growing Pains and our work are highly complementary:
1. **They assume stable item parameters; we test that assumption.** Their FPC framework relies on anchor item parameters not drifting. Our DIF analysis can identify when this assumption breaks down due to contamination.
2. **They optimize evaluation efficiency; we diagnose evaluation validity.** Growing Pains reduces the number of items needed; we identify which items should be trusted.
3. **Their acknowledged limitation is our research question.** They note "anchors may become contaminated or saturated over time, requiring recalibration" but do not address it. We provide the diagnostic tool for exactly this problem.
4. **Integration pathway**: DIF-flagged items could be excluded from Growing Pains' anchor sets, making their FPC calibration more robust to contamination.

### Kipnis et al. (2025) — METABENCH
- **Title**: MetaBench: A Sparse Benchmark for LLM Evaluation
- **Year**: 2025
- **Venue**: ICLR 2025
- **Key method/finding**: Distills six Open LLM Leaderboard benchmarks (ARC, GSM8K, HellaSwag, MMLU, TruthfulQA, WinoGrande) into <3% of their combined size using data from 5000+ LLMs. Uses Generalized Additive Models (GAM) to model subset-to-full-set relationships. Reconstructs benchmark scores with <0.9% MAE and leaderboard scores with <0.5% MAE. Provides two disjoint versions for repeated evaluation. Integrated into EleutherAI's lm-evaluation-harness.
- **Relevance to our paper**: METABENCH is our primary data source — we use their 5000+ model response matrices for IRT calibration and DIF analysis. Their item selection optimizes for predictive accuracy of aggregate scores; our DIF analysis adds a validity dimension by identifying which items remain measurement-invariant across model cohorts. Items selected by MetaBench that we flag as contaminated would suggest the sparse benchmark itself may be vulnerable to contamination effects.

### Li et al. (2024) — Contamination Detector
- **Title**: An Open-Source Data Contamination Report for Large Language Models
- **Year**: 2024
- **Venue**: Findings of EMNLP 2024, pp. 528–541
- **Authors**: Yucheng Li, Yunhao Guo, Frank Guerin, Chenghua Lin
- **Key method/finding**: Two-step contamination detection pipeline: (1) Bing Search API checks whether test items appear verbatim on the web (web-overlap detection), (2) human annotation classifies items as clean, input-only contaminated, or input-and-label contaminated. Provides 9,229 item-level web-overlap annotations for MMLU. Finds contamination levels ranging from 1% to 45% across six benchmarks, with contamination degree increasing rapidly over time. On MMLU, contamination causes only minimal accuracy increase despite substantial overlap.
- **Relevance to our paper**: **Primary ground truth source.** Their 9,229 item-level MMLU annotations provide the ground truth labels we use to validate DIF enrichment. Critical finding: enrichment ≈ 1.0 because their annotations capture *global* contamination (items available in Common Crawl accessible to all models), whereas DIF detects *differential* contamination (items that differentially advantage specific model cohorts). This global-vs-differential distinction is a key conceptual contribution of our work.

### Dekoninck et al. (2024) — ConStat
- **Title**: ConStat: Performance-Based Contamination Detection in Large Language Models
- **Year**: 2024
- **Venue**: NeurIPS 2024
- **Authors**: Jasper Dekoninck, Mark Niklas Müller, Martin Vechev
- **arXiv**: 2405.16281
- **Key method/finding**: Proposes a performance-based definition of contamination — defines contamination by its outcome (artificially inflated, non-generalizing benchmark performance) rather than its cause (training data overlap). Statistical test compares a model's performance on the target benchmark against reference benchmarks (rephrased samples, same-distribution samples, or different benchmarks for the same task). Achieves r² = 0.94 between estimated and ground-truth contamination effects. Finds high contamination levels in Mistral, Llama, Yi, and top Open LLM Leaderboard models.
- **Relevance to our paper**: ConStat and DIF are complementary population-level statistical approaches. ConStat detects whether a model's benchmark performance generalizes (performance anomaly); DIF detects whether specific items function differently across model cohorts (item-level anomaly). ConStat requires a reference benchmark for comparison; DIF requires only the original response matrix with temporal cohort labels. Together they cover both the model-level and item-level perspectives on contamination.

### Zhang et al. (2024) — GSM1K
- **Title**: A Careful Examination of Large Language Model Performance on Grade School Arithmetic
- **Year**: 2024
- **Venue**: NeurIPS 2024 (Datasets and Benchmarks Track)
- **Authors**: Hugh Zhang, Jeff Da, Dean Lee, Vaughn Robinson, Catherine Wu, Will Song, Tiffany Zhao, Pranav Raja, Dylan Slack, Qin Lyu, Sean Hendryx, Russell Kaplan, Michele Lunati, Summer Yue
- **arXiv**: 2405.00332
- **Key method/finding**: Creates GSM1K — 1,000 new grade-school math problems designed to mirror GSM8K's style and difficulty. Landmark empirical evidence of benchmark contamination: models show accuracy drops of up to 13 percentage points on fresh problems vs. GSM8K. Phi and Mistral families show systematic overfitting across almost all model sizes. Positive correlation (Spearman r² = 0.36) between a model's probability of generating GSM8K examples and its GSM8K-vs-GSM1K performance gap. Frontier models (GPT-4, Claude) show minimal memorization.
- **Relevance to our paper**: **Motivating example** for benchmark contamination as a real, quantifiable problem. The 10–13pp accuracy drops demonstrate that contamination materially distorts evaluation. Our DIF approach provides a complementary diagnostic: instead of creating a parallel benchmark (costly), DIF identifies which items in the *existing* benchmark are compromised, enabling in-situ contamination assessment.

- **Year**: 1993
- **Venue**: Psychometrika, 58(2), 159–194
- **Key method/finding**: Developed the SIBTEST procedure — a nonparametric, IRT model-based method that detects and estimates DIF without requiring item response function (IRF) estimation. Uses a multidimensional IRT model to explain how individual items combine to produce differential test functioning (DTF) at the test level. Employs a regression correction technique to control inflated Type I error while separating true bias from group ability differences.
- **Relevance to our paper**: SIBTEST is the foundational statistical test for detecting item-level bias across groups. Our DIF-based contamination detection adapts this logic: instead of demographic groups, we compare "pre-contamination" vs. "post-contamination" model cohorts. The multidimensional DIF framework directly informs our approach to separating genuine ability differences from item-specific anomalies.

### Clauser & Mazor (1998)
- **Title**: Using Statistical Procedures to Identify Differentially Functioning Test Items
- **Year**: 1998
- **Venue**: Educational Measurement: Issues and Practice, 17(1), 31–44
- **Key method/finding**: Comprehensive review of DIF detection methods including Mantel-Haenszel, logistic regression, and SIBTEST. Documents the landscape of statistical techniques for detecting items that function differently across groups while controlling for overall ability.
- **Relevance to our paper**: Provides the methodological taxonomy we draw from when selecting DIF detection procedures for the LLM benchmark setting. Establishes that multiple complementary DIF methods exist with different sensitivity profiles — motivating our multi-method approach.

### Zumbo (1999)
- **Title**: A Handbook on the Theory and Methods of Differential Item Functioning (DIF): Logistic Regression Modeling as a Unitary Framework for Binary and Likert-Type (Ordinal) Item Scores
- **Year**: 1999
- **Venue**: Technical report, Directorate of Human Resources Research and Evaluation, Department of National Defense, Ottawa, Canada
- **Key method/finding**: Presents logistic regression as a unifying framework for DIF analysis applicable to both binary and ordinal item scores. Provides theoretical grounding for understanding DIF as a violation of measurement invariance.

Zumbo's formalization of uniform vs. non-uniform DIF maps onto our distinction between items that are uniformly easier for contaminated models vs. items showing interaction effects with model ability.

### Holland & Wainer (1993)
- **Title**: Differential Item Functioning (edited volume)
- **Year**: 1993
- **Venue**: Lawrence Erlbaum Associates, Hillsdale, NJ

- **Year**: 2016
- **Venue**: EMNLP 2016, pp. 648–657

Demonstrates that IRT can describe characteristics of individual items (difficulty, discriminating power) and account for these in estimating NLP system ability. Applied to Recognizing Textual Entailment.

- **Title**: Learning Latent Parameters without Human Response Patterns: Item Response Theory with Artificial Crowds
- **Year**: 2019
- **Venue**: EMNLP-IJCNLP 2019, Hong Kong

Finds medium-to-large positive correlations between parameters learned from human vs. machine response patterns for NLI and sentiment analysis.

- **Title**: Comparing Test Sets with Item Response Theory
- **Year**: 2021
- **Venue**: ACL 2021
- **Key method/finding**: Evaluated 29 datasets using predictions from 18 pretrained Transformer models via IRT. Found that Quoref, HellaSwag, and MC-TACO best distinguish among SOTA models, while SNLI, MNLI, and CommitmentBank are saturated. - **Title**: Evaluation Examples Are Not Equally Informative: How Should That Change NLP Leaderboards?
- **Year**: 2021
- **Venue**: ACL-IJCNLP 2021
- **Key method/finding**: Creates a Bayesian IRT leaderboard model where latent subject skill and latent item difficulty predict correct responses. | **DIF analysis** | Not mentioned | Core methodology |
| **Granularity** | Dataset/benchmark level efficiency | Item-level contamination diagnostics |
| **Binary response** | Yes (limitation acknowledged) | Yes |

- **Title**: Learning Latent Parameters without Human Response Patterns: Item Response Theory with Artificial Crowds
- **Year**: 2019
- **Venue**: EMNLP-IJCNLP 2019, Hong Kong
- **Key method/finding**: Addresses the bottleneck of needing human response patterns to calibrate IRT models by proposing to learn IRT parameters from "artificial crowds" of DNN models. Finds medium-to-large positive correlations between parameters learned from human vs. machine response patterns for NLI and sentiment analysis.
- **Relevance to our paper**: Validates that IRT parameters estimated from machine (model) responses are meaningful and correlate with human-derived parameters. This justifies our use of LLM response matrices for IRT calibration.

### Vania et al. (2021)
- **Title**: Comparing Test Sets with Item Response Theory
- **Year**: 2021
- **Venue**: ACL 2021
- **Key method/finding**: Evaluated 29 datasets using predictions from 18 pretrained Transformer models via IRT. Found that Quoref, HellaSwag, and MC-TACO best distinguish among SOTA models, while SNLI, MNLI, and CommitmentBank are saturated. Provides a principled way to compare the discriminative quality of benchmark datasets.
- **Relevance to our paper**: Demonstrates IRT-based benchmark comparison at the dataset level. Our work extends this to item-level analysis across temporal model cohorts, using DIF to detect which specific items have degraded discriminative quality due to contamination.

### Rodriguez et al. (2021)
- **Title**: Evaluation Examples Are Not Equally Informative: How Should That Change NLP Leaderboards?
- **Year**: 2021
- **Venue**: ACL-IJCNLP 2021
- **Key method/finding**: Creates a Bayesian IRT leaderboard model where latent subject skill and latent item difficulty predict correct responses. Demonstrates that IRT can guide annotation priorities, identify annotation errors, detect overfitting, and identify the most informative evaluation examples. Released open-source IRT leaderboard code.
- **Relevance to our paper**: Directly relevant methodological predecessor. Their Bayesian IRT approach to leaderboards establishes that item-level modeling reveals evaluation quality issues invisible to aggregate scores. We build on this by using IRT-derived item parameters to detect contamination-induced parameter drift.

### Polo et al. (2024)
- **Title**: tinyBenchmarks: Evaluating LLMs with Fewer Examples
- **Year**: 2024
- **Venue**: ICML 2024
- **Key method/finding**: Shows that evaluating on ~100 curated IRT-selected items per benchmark is sufficient to accurately reproduce full-benchmark performance. Released IRT-based evaluation tools and tiny versions of Open LLM Leaderboard, MMLU, HELM, and AlpacaEval 2.0. Uses clustering-based item selection to ensure coverage of the difficulty/discrimination space.
- **Relevance to our paper**: tinyBenchmarks demonstrates the practical value of IRT for efficient evaluation. Their item selection methodology (clustering IRT representations) is adopted by Growing Pains for anchor selection. Our DIF analysis provides a complementary diagnostic: not just which items are informative, but which items have become unreliable due to contamination.

---

## 3. Contamination Detection

### Shi et al. (2024)
- **Title**: Detecting Pretraining Data from Large Language Models
- **Year**: 2024
- **Venue**: ICLR 2024
- **Key method/finding**: Proposes MIN-K% PROB — a membership inference method that identifies pretraining data by checking whether the k% of tokens with minimum probability under the LLM are unlikely enough. Introduces the WIKIMIA benchmark for evaluation. Achieves 7.4% improvement over prior methods. Applied to copyrighted book detection, contaminated example detection, and privacy auditing.
- **Relevance to our paper**: Min-K% operates at the instance level (is this text in the training data?) while our DIF approach operates at the item level across model populations (does this item behave differently for likely-contaminated models?). The approaches are complementary: Min-K% requires model access per instance; DIF requires only response matrices.

### Zhang et al. (2024) — Min-K%++
- **Title**: Min-K%++: Improved Baseline for Detecting Pre-Training Data from Large Language Models
- **Year**: 2024
- **Venue**: ICLR 2025
- **Key method/finding**: Extends Min-K% by measuring how sharply peaked the likelihood is around the input (analogous to curvature), using second-order statistics motivated by the connection between maximum likelihood training and the Hessian trace via score matching. More robust than zeroth-order signals.
- **Relevance to our paper**: Further develops the instance-level contamination detection paradigm. Our work offers an orthogonal, population-level signal that does not require per-instance likelihood computation.

### Balloccu et al. (2024)
- **Title**: Leak, Cheat, Repeat: Data Contamination and Evaluation Malpractices in Closed-Source LLMs
- **Year**: 2024
- **Venue**: EACL 2024
- **Key method/finding**: Systematic review of 255 papers using ChatGPT/GPT-4, documenting that over 4.7M samples from 263 datasets were exposed through the web interface. Catalogs evaluation malpractices including unfair baselines, reproducibility issues, and lack of contamination awareness.
- **Relevance to our paper**: Establishes the scale and severity of the contamination problem. Their documentation of widespread data leakage motivates our work: if contamination is pervasive and hard to prevent, we need methods to detect and account for it post-hoc — exactly what DIF provides.

### Golchin & Surdeanu (2024)
- **Title**: Data Contamination Quiz: A Tool to Detect and Estimate Contamination in Large Language Models
- **Year**: 2024
- **Venue**: TACL 2024
- **Key method/finding**: Frames contamination detection as a multiple-choice quiz: given an original instance and three word-level perturbations, a contaminated model should identify the original. Achieves 92–100% accuracy across seven datasets. Detects specific contamination in AG News, WNLI, and XSum for GPT-4.
- **Relevance to our paper**: DCQ is a clever per-model, per-instance detection method but requires generating perturbations and querying the model. Our DIF approach is purely observational — it works from existing response matrices without additional model queries or perturbation generation.

### Oren et al. (2024)
- **Title**: Proving Test Set Contamination in Black Box Language Models
- **Year**: 2024
- **Venue**: ICLR 2024
- **Key method/finding**: Statistical test comparing likelihood of a benchmark's canonical ordering vs. shuffled versions. Contaminated models find canonical orderings more likely due to memorized example order. Provides exact false positive guarantees without requiring access to pretraining data or model weights. Effective on models as small as 1.4B parameters with only 1000 examples.
- **Relevance to our paper**: Elegant black-box method with formal statistical guarantees. However, it detects dataset-level contamination (is the whole benchmark memorized?) rather than item-level contamination effects (which specific items are affected?). Our DIF approach provides item-level granularity. Notably, canonical ordering 检验是 population-level 方法，与 DIF 更近（都是统计检验方法检测污染），区别在于 Oren 检测记忆顺序而 DIF 检测 differential performance。

### Li et al. (2024) — Contamination Detector
- **Title**: An Open-Source Data Contamination Report for Large Language Models
- **Year**: 2024
- **Venue**: Findings of EMNLP 2024, pp. 528–541
- **Authors**: Yucheng Li, Yunhao Guo, Frank Guerin, Chenghua Lin
- **Key method/finding**: Two-step contamination detection pipeline: (1) Bing Search API checks whether test items appear verbatim on the web (web-overlap detection), (2) human annotation classifies items as clean, input-only contaminated, or input-and-label contaminated. Provides 9,229 item-level web-overlap annotations for MMLU. Finds contamination levels ranging from 1% to 45% across six benchmarks, with contamination degree increasing rapidly over time. On MMLU, contamination causes only minimal accuracy increase despite substantial overlap.
- **Relevance to our paper**: **Primary ground truth source.** Their 9,229 item-level MMLU annotations provide the ground truth labels we use to validate DIF enrichment. Critical finding: enrichment ≈ 1.0 because their annotations capture *global* contamination (items available in Common Crawl accessible to all models), whereas DIF detects *differential* contamination (items that differentially advantage specific model cohorts). This global-vs-differential distinction is a key conceptual contribution of our work.

### Dekoninck et al. (2024) — ConStat
- **Title**: ConStat: Performance-Based Contamination Detection in Large Language Models
- **Year**: 2024
- **Venue**: NeurIPS 2024
- **Authors**: Jasper Dekoninck, Mark Niklas Müller, Martin Vechev
- **arXiv**: 2405.16281
- **Key method/finding**: Proposes a performance-based definition of contamination — defines contamination by its outcome (artificially inflated, non-generalizing benchmark performance) rather than its cause (training data overlap). Statistical test compares a model's performance on the target benchmark against reference benchmarks (rephrased samples, same-distribution samples, or different benchmarks for the same task). Achieves r² = 0.94 between estimated and ground-truth contamination effects. Finds high contamination levels in Mistral, Llama, Yi, and top Open LLM Leaderboard models.
- **Relevance to our paper**: ConStat and DIF are complementary population-level statistical approaches. ConStat detects whether a model's benchmark performance generalizes (performance anomaly); DIF detects whether specific items function differently across model cohorts (item-level anomaly). ConStat requires a reference benchmark for comparison; DIF requires only the original response matrix with temporal cohort labels. Together they cover both the model-level and item-level perspectives on contamination.

### Zhang et al. (2024) — GSM1K
- **Title**: A Careful Examination of Large Language Model Performance on Grade School Arithmetic
- **Year**: 2024
- **Venue**: NeurIPS 2024 (Datasets and Benchmarks Track)
- **Authors**: Hugh Zhang, Jeff Da, Dean Lee, Vaughn Robinson, Catherine Wu, Will Song, Tiffany Zhao, Pranav Raja, Dylan Slack, Qin Lyu, Sean Hendryx, Russell Kaplan, Michele Lunati, Summer Yue
- **arXiv**: 2405.00332
- **Key method/finding**: Creates GSM1K — 1,000 new grade-school math problems designed to mirror GSM8K's style and difficulty. Landmark empirical evidence of benchmark contamination: models show accuracy drops of up to 13 percentage points on fresh problems vs. GSM8K. Phi and Mistral families show systematic overfitting across almost all model sizes. Positive correlation (Spearman r² = 0.36) between a model's probability of generating GSM8K examples and its GSM8K-vs-GSM1K performance gap. Frontier models (GPT-4, Claude) show minimal memorization.
- **Relevance to our paper**: **Motivating example** for benchmark contamination as a real, quantifiable problem. The 10–13pp accuracy drops demonstrate that contamination materially distorts evaluation. Our DIF approach provides a complementary diagnostic: instead of creating a parallel benchmark (costly), DIF identifies which items in the *existing* benchmark are compromised, enabling in-situ contamination assessment.

### Deng et al. (2024)
- **Title**: Investigating Data Contamination in Modern Benchmarks for Large Language Models
- **Year**: 2024
- **Venue**: NAACL 2024, pp. 8706–8719
- **Key method/finding**: Proposes two methods: a retrieval-based system to find overlaps between benchmarks and pretraining corpora (for open-source LLMs), and Testset Slot Guessing (TS-Guessing) for proprietary LLMs. Finds ChatGPT and GPT-4 achieve 52% and 57% exact match rates in guessing missing MMLU options.
- **Relevance to our paper**: Demonstrates contamination in the exact benchmark (MMLU) we analyze. Their TS-Guessing evidence of MMLU contamination in GPT-4 provides ground-truth validation context for our DIF-based detection.

---

## 4. Dynamic/Adaptive Benchmarks

### Zhu et al. (2024a) — DyVal
- **Title**: DyVal: Dynamic Evaluation of Large Language Models for Reasoning Tasks
- **Year**: 2024
- **Venue**: ICLR 2024
- **Key method/finding**: Generates evaluation tasks at test time using graph-based complexity control to mitigate memorization. Applies graph complexity metrics to parameterize reasoning problem difficulty. Dynamically constructs evaluation instances rather than relying on static test sets.
- **Relevance to our paper**: Represents the "regenerate the benchmark" approach to contamination. Our work takes the complementary "detect and account for contamination in existing benchmarks" approach, which preserves historical comparability.

### Zhu et al. (2024b) — DyVal 2
- **Title**: Dynamic Evaluation of Large Language Models by Meta Probing Agents
- **Year**: 2024
- **Venue**: arXiv:2402.14865
- **Key method/finding**: Extends DyVal with Meta Probing Agents (MPA) inspired by psychometrics. Agents automatically transform original evaluation problems targeting three cognitive abilities: language understanding, problem solving, and domain knowledge. More generalizable than task-specific dynamic generation.
- **Relevance to our paper**: MPA's psychometric inspiration is conceptually aligned with our IRT-based approach, but they use psychometrics to generate new items while we use it to analyze existing items for contamination signals.

### White et al. (2024) — LiveBench
- **Title**: LiveBench: A Challenging, Contamination-Free LLM Benchmark
- **Year**: 2024
- **Venue**: arXiv:2406.19314
- **Key method/finding**: Releases new questions monthly based on recent datasets, arXiv papers, news, and IMDb synopses. All questions have verifiable, objective ground-truth answers enabling automatic scoring without LLM judges. Spans 18 tasks across 6 categories (Math, Reasoning, Data Analysis, Language, Coding, Instruction Following).
- **Relevance to our paper**: LiveBench's monthly refresh strategy prevents contamination prospectively. Our DIF method detects contamination retrospectively in static benchmarks. The approaches address different temporal windows: LiveBench prevents future contamination; we diagnose past contamination in widely-used benchmarks whose historical results we want to preserve.

### Wang et al. (2024) — MMLU-Pro
- **Title**: MMLU-Pro: A More Robust and Challenging Multi-Task Language Understanding Benchmark
- **Year**: 2024
- **Venue**: NeurIPS 2024
- **Key method/finding**: Enhances MMLU with harder, reasoning-focused questions and increases answer choices from 4 to 10, reducing random guessing success. Over 12K questions across 14 domains. GPT-4o achieves only 72.6%, and the gap between GPT-4o and GPT-4-Turbo widens from 1% (MMLU) to 9% (MMLU-Pro), showing better discriminative power.
- **Relevance to our paper**: MMLU-Pro addresses contamination by making a harder benchmark, but doesn't diagnose which original MMLU items are compromised. Our DIF analysis can quantify exactly which MMLU items have degraded, providing evidence for why harder replacements are needed and which content areas are most affected.

### Gema et al. (2024) — MMLU-Redux
- **Title**: Are We Done with MMLU?
- **Year**: 2024
- **Venue**: arXiv:2406.04127
- **Key method/finding**: Manual re-annotation of 5,700 MMLU questions reveals a 6.5% error rate. Error types include parsing mistakes, multiple correct answers, and missing context. Virology subset has 57% errors. Re-evaluation with corrected labels shows significant metric discrepancies and ranking shifts.
- **Relevance to our paper**: MMLU-Redux addresses data quality while our work addresses contamination — both are sources of measurement error. Items flagged by DIF analysis that are not contaminated may instead have quality issues, making these analyses complementary.

---

## 5. Key Technical Comparisons

### Habba, Itzhak, Yehudai, Perlitz, Bandel, Shmueli-Scheuer, Choshen & Stanovsky (2026) — Growing Pains
- **Title**: Growing Pains: Extensible and Efficient LLM Benchmarking Via Fixed Parameter Calibration
- **Year**: 2026 (April)
- **Venue**: arXiv:2604.12843
- **Authors**: Eliya Habba, Itay Itzhak, Asaf Yehudai, Yotam Perlitz, Elron Bandel, Michal Shmueli-Scheuer, Leshem Choshen, Gabriel Stanovsky

#### Method Details
- **IRT Model**: Multidimensional 2PL IRT (MIRT-2PL). Each item has a discrimination vector **a_i** and intercept **d_i**.
- **Calibration**: Fixed Parameter Calibration (FPC) — previously calibrated item parameters are held fixed; only new item parameters are estimated when new benchmarks are added.
- **Anchor Selection**: Clustering-based method (following Polo et al.) that distributes anchors across the difficulty/discrimination space. Uses 100 anchor items per dataset. Outperforms top-K discrimination selection.
- **Scale**: 400+ models, evaluated on Open LLM Leaderboard (ARC, GSM8K, HellaSwag, MMLU, TruthfulQA, WinoGrande) and MMLU's 57 subjects.
- **Performance**: Predicts full-evaluation performance within 2–3 percentage points; Spearman ρ ≥ 0.9 for ranking preservation.

#### Technical Comparison with Our Approach

| Dimension | Growing Pains | Our DIF Approach |
|-----------|---------------|------------------|
| **Goal** | Efficient, extensible benchmarking via FPC | Detect contamination-induced measurement distortion |
| **IRT model** | MIRT-2PL | 2PL (with DIF extensions) |
| **Core technique** | Fixed parameter calibration with anchor items | DIF analysis across temporal model cohorts |
| **Contamination** | Acknowledged as limitation ("anchors may become contaminated or saturated over time, requiring recalibration") but **not addressed** | Central focus — DIF detects which items are affected |
| **Item drift** | Not detected; assumes item parameters are stable | Explicitly models item parameter drift as DIF signal |
| **DIF analysis** | Not mentioned | Core methodology |
| **Granularity** | Dataset/benchmark level efficiency | Item-level contamination diagnostics |
| **Binary response** | Yes (limitation acknowledged) | Yes |

#### Complementarity
Growing Pains and our work are highly complementary:
1. **They assume stable item parameters; we test that assumption.** Their FPC framework relies on anchor item parameters not drifting. Our DIF analysis can identify when this assumption breaks down due to contamination.
2. **They optimize evaluation efficiency; we diagnose evaluation validity.** Growing Pains reduces the number of items needed; we identify which items should be trusted.
3. **Their acknowledged limitation is our research question.** They note "anchors may become contaminated or saturated over time, requiring recalibration" but do not address it. We provide the diagnostic tool for exactly this problem.
4. **Integration pathway**: DIF-flagged items could be excluded from Growing Pains' anchor sets, making their FPC calibration more robust to contamination.

### Kipnis et al. (2025) — METABENCH
- **Title**: MetaBench: A Sparse Benchmark for LLM Evaluation
- **Year**: 2025
- **Venue**: ICLR 2025
- **Key method/finding**: Distills six Open LLM Leaderboard benchmarks (ARC, GSM8K, HellaSwag, MMLU, TruthfulQA, WinoGrande) into <3% of their combined size using data from 5000+ LLMs. Uses Generalized Additive Models (GAM) to model subset-to-full-set relationships. Reconstructs benchmark scores with <0.9% MAE and leaderboard scores with <0.5% MAE. Provides two disjoint versions for repeated evaluation. Integrated into EleutherAI's lm-evaluation-harness.
- **Relevance to our paper**: METABENCH is our primary data source — we use their 5000+ model response matrices for IRT calibration and DIF analysis. Their item selection optimizes for predictive accuracy of aggregate scores; our DIF analysis adds a validity dimension by identifying which items remain measurement-invariant across model cohorts. Items selected by MetaBench that we flag as contaminated would suggest the sparse benchmark itself may be vulnerable to contamination effects.

- **Relevance to our paper**: Demonstrates contamination in the exact benchmark (MMLU) we analyze. Their TS-Guessing evidence of MMLU contamination in GPT-4 provides ground-truth validation context for our DIF-based detection.
+### Tao, Wang et al. (2025) — Self-Critique
+- **Title**: Detecting Data Contamination from Reinforcement Learning Post-training for Large Language Models
+- **Venue**: arXiv:2510.09259 (submitted Oct 2025, revised Mar 2026)
+- **Authors**: Yongding Tao, Tian Wang, Yihong Dong, Huanyu Liu, Kechi Zhang, Xiaolong Hu, Ge Li

+- **Key method/finding**: First systematic study of contamination detection in the RL post-training phase. Proposes Self-Critique, motivated by the observation that RL training causes output entropy distribution to collapse into highly specific, sparse modes. Outperforms existing detection methods on AIME, K&K, SAT, GSM8K benchmarks.
